text: A ronin says he did not do it, and there is nobody in his life whose word could settle the matter. Masahiro Makino spends 135 minutes inside that gap, which is long for 1929 and changes what the film is for: not the clearing of a name but a slow account of who will listen, and on what terms, to a man with no house behind him. Japanese cinema in 1929 could not record a voice, so the protest reaches an audience the way it reaches the villagers, read off a face rather than heard. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of the year. Innocence, in this account of it, is never a fact waiting to be dug up; it is a claim that has to be carried in person through rooms where the decision has already been taken.

The scheme is patient: let the man who killed for an inheritance go on receiving evidence that the woman he killed is still at home. Hye-sook has her reason. Her fiancé was driving Ji-young that night and died as an afterthought to somebody else's arithmetic, so she builds the illusion and then stays inside it, close enough to watch it work. Ninety-five minutes, South Korea, 1970. Chung Jin-woo runs it as a two-hander in which the one doing the punishing has to stay near the one being punished, feeding the deception daily, and proximity does what proximity does. Baeksang gave it best film. The interest is in the upkeep — a ghost that has to be manufactured every morning by someone who must keep her face straight while she does it.

The work is henequen, the field is in Mexico, and the hands are Korean. The year is 1905, and Kim Ho-sun gives 148 minutes to what that arrangement does to the people inside it. Threaded through the rows is a courtship between two whose families would never have permitted the introduction: a daughter of an aristocratic house that has already lost its money, and a butcher's son. In Korea that distance was structural, maintained by everybody at once. On a plantation it has to be argued again each day by two people doing identical work under identical supervision, which is not the same as its disappearance. It took the Grand Bell for best film. How long a hierarchy survives being shipped abroad is the question the film keeps returning to.

The terms were plain: say the words that take it back, or be executed. Catholicism arrived in Korea in 1784 and the state answered with a procedure for extracting renunciation — pain applied until a sentence comes out, the sentence being the point rather than anything it reports. Choi Ha-won follows Seung-hun and her brother, who go on spreading the thing regardless. Over 110 minutes the costume drama becomes a study of an asymmetry: the accused is asked not what happened but what is held to be true, and everyone present understands that a recantation under torture is worthless as evidence and enormous as ritual. Made in 1981, it took the Grand Bell for best film. What it returns to is the machinery — who is brought in, who asks, what counts as the answer that ends the session.

A man arrives in Grabovica calling himself a journalist, and the news he carries is that the school will close. There are not enough children in the region to keep it open. In a village where the days have run the same way for a long time, an administrative sentence like that works like a bar under a floorboard, and the place comes up along seams nobody had marked. Bahrudin 'Bato' Čengić made it for Yugoslav television in 1985, eighty-four minutes, and he lets two kinds of report move through the same streets: one that arrives with a stranger and can in principle be checked, and one that arrives from nowhere and cannot. Rumour is the medium, and the film is unusually precise about how a small population settles on what to believe.

The World Cup came to Argentina in 1978, and while it was on, the dictatorship decided that one neighbourhood would be removed. Manuel Dorrego, known as the Hidden City. The residents did not accept the decision, and their resistance is what Osvaldo Andéchaga puts on screen in seventy-five minutes, eleven years after the fact. That compression is the best instinct in it: no decades, no panorama, only the stretch of time in which an eradication order meets the households it names. Read as history the episode is a clause in a paragraph about the junta. Filmed at this scale it is an address, a queue, a family sorting what can be carried. The Silver Condor went to it as best film. Andéchaga keeps the argument at street level, where the order had to be enforced.

Eighteen minutes, one farm, and a full year of waiting to get them. Christopher Chapman shot on his parents' land at Lake Simcoe and cut the result to Vivaldi, which is either a shortcut or the whole idea, since the music already knows where a year is going and leaves the camera free to look. What it looks at is small: ground, weather, the changes a familiar place makes when nobody is arranging them. A 1953 documentary this short, made at home, is under no obligation to explain Canada to anyone, and can stay at the scale of one field seen four ways. The borrowed structure keeps it from being a home movie. The home keeps the structure from being an exercise. Seventy years on, the restraint is what carries it.

Rouzbeh was wounded in a war, and the wound is not finished with him. His condition is worsening, hospital is the next step, and Yalda's marriage stops being something conducted at home and becomes a matter of admission desks and other people's hours. Ahmad Reza Mo'tamedi takes 111 minutes and spends them where this kind of story is usually quickest: the stretch in which a wife who loves her husband begins, privately, to doubt. The war itself is nowhere on screen. It survives in a body, in a schedule of treatment, in the way a room reorganises itself around one person's needs. It took the Crystal Simorgh for best film. Care without an end date makes an odd engine for a drama, since nothing escalates and yet every day arrives with its demand.

A journalist is handed a subject and sent out: a Communist leader, living in the South, after the war. Im Kwon-taek builds the investigation in ninety-six minutes, brisk for a life assembled out of other people's testimony, and the speed is part of the method, since the man arrives in fragments, each handed over by someone with a stake in how he comes out. What the reporter gathers is less a biography than a set of positions people have taken about him. It won the Grand Bell for best film. Reconstruction is the form and the trap at once: every account doubles as an alibi for whoever gives it, and by the end of a session the film has learned as much about the person answering as about the person described.

A documentary shot in the present tense about something its own description already puts in the past. F.R. Crawley filmed Newfoundland in 1951 on the understanding that the life in front of the lens was nearly gone, and forty-five minutes is a long stretch for a portrait and a very short one for a place. The tension between those two facts is the discipline of it: what earns a shot when the criterion is not interest but disappearance. Nothing is argued. People do their work and the camera stays with the work instead of cutting away to a conclusion about it. Films made under that instruction age strangely, flatter than they should be at the time and worth more later, because the ordinary business nobody thought needed recording is the part that cannot be got back.

Half past nine on the morning of 9 September 2011, in a courtroom beside the Wenyu River, and the people who came for the verdict are standing outside it. Wang Lihong was charged with picking quarrels and provoking trouble. Ai Xiaoming filmed the day around that phrase, friends gathered at the scene again, lawyers and citizen journalists and artists, and gave forty-three minutes to what they were willing to say while it was going on. The proceeding is not the subject. The gathering is: who turns up, what a person will let a camera record, how a crowd conducts itself when its only available act is to be counted. It follows an earlier film of hers, Let Sunshine Reach the Ground, and keeps the method, which is to be present where presence is the contested thing.
